claim: Chronic loss of Augmenter of Liver Regeneration (ALR) results in mitochondrial myopathy with cataracts.
source: Chronic loss of Augmenter of Liver Regeneration (ALR) results in mitochondrial myopathy with cataracts; however, the mechanism for this disorder remains unclear.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature describing this clinical phenotype.

claim: Loss of ALR results in impaired cytosolic Fe/S cluster biogenesis in mammalian cells.
source: Here, we demonstrate that loss of ALR, a principal component of the MIA40/ALR protein import pathway, results in impaired cytosolic Fe/S cluster biogenesis in mammalian cells.
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental measurements of cytosolic Fe/S cluster markers (GPAT, XO, cytosolic aconitase) in cells with ALR downregulation.

claim: MIA40/ALR facilitates the mitochondrial import of ABCB8 through physical interaction.
source: Mechanistically, MIA40/ALR facilitates the mitochondrial import of ATP-binding cassette (ABC)-B8, an inner mitochondrial membrane protein required for cytoplasmic Fe/S cluster maturation, through physical interaction with ABCB8.
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments showing physical interaction between MIA40 and ABCB8, and import assays showing reduced mitochondrial ABCB8 with ALR/MIA40 downregulation.

claim: Downregulation of ALR impairs mitochondrial ABCB8 import.
source: Downregulation of ALR impairs mitochondrial ABCB8 import, reduces cytoplasmic Fe/S cluster maturation, and increases cellular iron through the iron regulatory protein-iron response element system.
evidence: Demonstrated through mitochondrial fractionation and import assays showing reduced mitochondrial ABCB8 levels with ALR downregulation.

claim: Downregulation of ALR reduces cytoplasmic Fe/S cluster maturation.
source: Downregulation of ALR impairs mitochondrial ABCB8 import, reduces cytoplasmic Fe/S cluster maturation, and increases cellular iron through the iron regulatory protein-iron response element system.
evidence: Supported by measurements of GPAT protein levels, XO activity, and cytosolic aconitase activity in ALR-downregulated cells.

claim: Downregulation of ALR increases cellular iron through the IRP-IRE system.
source: Downregulation of ALR impairs mitochondrial ABCB8 import, reduces cytoplasmic Fe/S cluster maturation, and increases cellular iron through the iron regulatory protein-iron response element system.
evidence: Demonstrated through measurements of Tfrc mRNA levels, transferrin-mediated iron uptake, and luciferase reporter assays showing IRP1-dependent regulation.

claim: Several mutations in ALR have been described for mitochondrial myopathy and cataract disorder.
source: Chronic loss of Augmenter of Liver Regeneration (ALR) results in mitochondrial myopathy and cataract, and combined respiratory chain deficiency (Di Fonzo et al., 2009; Calderwood et al., 2016; Nambot et al., 2017). Several mutations in ALR have been described for this disorder.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature describing ALR mutations in patients.

claim: Some ALR mutations result in premature stop codons.
source: Some of these documented mutations result in premature stop codon, while the R194H mutation has been shown to affect the protein stability through increasing dissociation of its cofactor FAD (Daithankar et al., 2010; Nambot et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature describing specific ALR mutations.

claim: The R194H mutation in ALR affects protein stability by increasing dissociation of its cofactor FAD.
source: Some of these documented mutations result in premature stop codon, while the R194H mutation has been shown to affect the protein stability through increasing dissociation of its cofactor FAD (Daithankar et al., 2010; Nambot et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature characterizing the R194H mutation.

claim: R194H mutant ALR is not functional.
source: Cellular studies demonstrated that R194H mutant ALR is not functional, and mutant cells can be complemented by ectopic expression of wild type (WT) ALR (Di Fonzo et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to published cellular studies of the R194H mutation.

claim: Mutant ALR cells can be complemented by ectopic expression of wild type ALR.
source: Cellular studies demonstrated that R194H mutant ALR is not functional, and mutant cells can be complemented by ectopic expression of wild type (WT) ALR (Di Fonzo et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to published complementation studies.

claim: ALR is a sulfhydryl oxidase with two isoforms.
source: ALR is a sulfhydryl oxidase with two isoforms – a full-length isoform that is predominantly in the mitochondria, but has also been observed in other locations depending on the cell type, and a shorter cytosolic isoform (Ibrahim and Weiss, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature and confirmed by subcellular fractionation experiments in this study.

claim: The full-length isoform of ALR is predominantly in the mitochondria.
source: ALR is a sulfhydryl oxidase with two isoforms – a full-length isoform that is predominantly in the mitochondria, but has also been observed in other locations depending on the cell type, and a shorter cytosolic isoform (Ibrahim and Weiss, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation and confirmed by subcellular fractionation shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The cytosolic isoform of ALR lacks the first 80 amino acids.
source: The cytosolic isoform of ALR, which is thought to function in hepatic regeneration (Li et al., 2002; Ibrahim and Weiss, 2019), lacks the first 80 amino acids, but retains the catalytic domain necessary to oxidize cysteines.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature describing ALR isoforms.

claim: The cytosolic isoform of ALR retains the catalytic domain necessary to oxidize cysteines.
source: The cytosolic isoform of ALR, which is thought to function in hepatic regeneration (Li et al., 2002; Ibrahim and Weiss, 2019), lacks the first 80 amino acids, but retains the catalytic domain necessary to oxidize cysteines.
evidence: Based on known structural features of ALR isoforms from published literature.

claim: The full-length isoform of ALR localizes to the mitochondrial intermembrane space.
source: Within the mitochondria, the full-length isoform of ALR localizes to the mitochondrial intermembrane space.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of ALR localization within mitochondria.

claim: ALR has been implicated in hepatic regeneration after injury.
source: Although the function of ALR is not entirely understood, it has been implicated in hepatic regeneration after injury (Polimeno et al., 2011), protection against hepatic and renal injury (Huang et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2019), facilitation of cardiac development (Dabir et al., 2013), and maintenance of embryonic stem cells (Todd et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: ALR has been implicated in protection against hepatic and renal injury.
source: Although the function of ALR is not entirely understood, it has been implicated in hepatic regeneration after injury (Polimeno et al., 2011), protection against hepatic and renal injury (Huang et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2019), facilitation of cardiac development (Dabir et al., 2013), and maintenance of embryonic stem cells (Todd et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: ALR has been implicated in facilitation of cardiac development.
source: Although the function of ALR is not entirely understood, it has been implicated in hepatic regeneration after injury (Polimeno et al., 2011), protection against hepatic and renal injury (Huang et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2019), facilitation of cardiac development (Dabir et al., 2013), and maintenance of embryonic stem cells (Todd et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: ALR has been implicated in maintenance of embryonic stem cells.
source: Although the function of ALR is not entirely understood, it has been implicated in hepatic regeneration after injury (Polimeno et al., 2011), protection against hepatic and renal injury (Huang et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2019), facilitation of cardiac development (Dabir et al., 2013), and maintenance of embryonic stem cells (Todd et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Mice with liver-specific deletion of ALR from birth develop steatohepatitis and hepatocellular carcinoma.
source: Mice with liver-specific deletion of ALR from birth develop steatohepatitis and hepatocellular carcinoma and have exacerbated hepatic injury when exposed to alcohol, while postnatal deletion of ALR in the liver induces oxidative stress and promotes hepatic steatosis (Gandhi et al., 2015; Kumar et al., 2016; Kumar et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published mouse studies.

claim: Mice with liver-specific deletion of ALR from birth have exacerbated hepatic injury when exposed to alcohol.
source: Mice with liver-specific deletion of ALR from birth develop steatohepatitis and hepatocellular carcinoma and have exacerbated hepatic injury when exposed to alcohol, while postnatal deletion of ALR in the liver induces oxidative stress and promotes hepatic steatosis (Gandhi et al., 2015; Kumar et al., 2016; Kumar et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published mouse studies.

claim: Postnatal deletion of ALR in the liver induces oxidative stress and promotes hepatic steatosis.
source: Mice with liver-specific deletion of ALR from birth develop steatohepatitis and hepatocellular carcinoma and have exacerbated hepatic injury when exposed to alcohol, while postnatal deletion of ALR in the liver induces oxidative stress and promotes hepatic steatosis (Gandhi et al., 2015; Kumar et al., 2016; Kumar et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published mouse studies.

claim: Ectopic expression of mitochondria-targeted human ALR rescues cytoplasmic iron-sulfur cluster maturation defects in Erv1-null yeast.
source: Previous studies demonstrated that ectopic expression of mitochondria-targeted human ALR rescues the cytoplasmic iron-sulfur (Fe/S) cluster maturation defects in Erv1-null yeast (Lange et al., 2001), suggesting that ALR may be the functional homolog of yeast Erv1p and play a role in Fe/S cluster biogenesis.
evidence: Supported by citation to published yeast complementation studies.

claim: The defects of cytosolic Fe/S clusters in Erv1-null yeast may be related to a second mutation leading to decreased glutathione levels.
source: However, a recent paper demonstrated that the defects of cytosolic Fe/S clusters in Erv1-null yeast may be related to a second mutation leading to decreased glutathione levels (Ozer et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to published yeast study.

claim: The synthesis of Fe/S clusters occurs in the mitochondria on the scaffold protein ISCU.
source: The synthesis of Fe/S clusters occurs in the mitochondria on the scaffold protein iron-sulfur cluster assembly enzyme (ISCU).
evidence: Based on established knowledge of Fe/S cluster biogenesis.

claim: Iron destined for Fe/S cluster synthesis is imported into mitochondria by mitoferrin 1/2.
source: Iron destined for Fe/S cluster synthesis is imported into mitochondria by mitoferrin 1/2 and is delivered to ISCU by frataxin.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of mitochondrial iron metabolism.

claim: Iron is delivered to ISCU by frataxin.
source: Iron destined for Fe/S cluster synthesis is imported into mitochondria by mitoferrin 1/2 and is delivered to ISCU by frataxin.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of Fe/S cluster assembly.

claim: ABCB7 and ABCB8 are the two mammalian mitochondrial transporters thought to be critical for cytosolic Fe/S cluster maturation.
source: To date, ABCB7 and ABCB8 are the two mammalian mitochondrial transporters thougth to be critial for cytosolic Fe/S cluster maturation (Ichikawa et al., 2012; Ye and Rouault, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature on ABCB7 and ABCB8.

claim: Deletion of Abcb8 in mouse heart leads to cytosolic Fe/S cluster deficiency and spontaneous cardiomyopathy.
source: Deletion of Abcb8 in mouse heart leads to cytosolic Fe/S cluster deficiency and spontaneous cardiomyopathy (Ichikawa et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to published mouse study.

claim: Conditional deletion of Iop1 in mice results in complete lethality.
source: Conditional deletion of Iop1, one component of CIA machinery, in mice results in complete lethality, and deletion of this gene in mouse embryonic fibroblasts leads to cellular iron accumulation and rapid cell death (Song and Lee, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to published mouse study.

claim: Deletion of Iop1 in mouse embryonic fibroblasts leads to cellular iron accumulation and rapid cell death.
source: Conditional deletion of Iop1, one component of CIA machinery, in mice results in complete lethality, and deletion of this gene in mouse embryonic fibroblasts leads to cellular iron accumulation and rapid cell death (Song and Lee, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to published cell study.

claim: Erv1 mediates cytosolic Fe/S cluster biogenesis in the parasitic trypanosome T. brucei.
source: Additionally, Erv1 has also been shown to mediate cytosolic Fe/S cluster biogenesis in the parasitic trypanosome T. brucei (Haindrich et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study in T. brucei.

claim: In the iron-replete state, IRP1 acquires an Fe/S cluster and functions as a cytosolic aconitase.
source: In the iron-replete state, IRP1 acquires an Fe/S cluster and functions as a cytosolic aconitase, while IRP2 is proteolytically degraded in an iron- and oxygen-dependent process.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of IRP regulation.

claim: In the iron-replete state, IRP2 is proteolytically degraded in an iron- and oxygen-dependent process.
source: In the iron-replete state, IRP1 acquires an Fe/S cluster and functions as a cytosolic aconitase, while IRP2 is proteolytically degraded in an iron- and oxygen-dependent process.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of IRP regulation.

claim: In the iron-starved state, IRP1 loses its Fe/S cluster and becomes activated.
source: In the iron-starved state, IRP1 loses its Fe/S cluster and becomes activated, and IRP2 is stabilized.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of IRP regulation.

claim: In the iron-starved state, IRP2 is stabilized.
source: In the iron-starved state, IRP1 loses its Fe/S cluster and becomes activated, and IRP2 is stabilized.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of IRP regulation.

claim: In yeast, Erv1p, together with Mia40, is part of the oxidative folding machinery required for the import of a subset of mitochondrial proteins.
source: In yeast, Erv1p, together with Mia40, is part of the oxidative folding machinery required for the import of a subset of mitochondrial proteins.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of yeast mitochondrial protein import.

claim: Mia40 oxidizes the cysteine residues within imported proteins.
source: Mia40 oxidizes the cysteine residues within imported proteins, and the reduced Mia40 is re-oxidized by Erv1p, effectively recycling Mia40 for further use (Müller et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature on Mia40/Erv1p mechanism.

claim: Reduced Mia40 is re-oxidized by Erv1p.
source: Mia40 oxidizes the cysteine residues within imported proteins, and the reduced Mia40 is re-oxidized by Erv1p, effectively recycling Mia40 for further use (Müller et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature on Mia40/Erv1p mechanism.

claim: A similar electron transfer process has been demonstrated using recombinant human MIA40 and ALR proteins.
source: A similar electron transfer process has also been demonstrated using recombinant human MIA40 and ALR proteins (Banci et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to published biochemical study.

claim: Downregulation of Alr in MEFs results in a significant reduction of Alr at the mRNA level.
source: To elucidate the role of ALR in cytosolic Fe/S cluster maturation and mitochondrial function in mammalian cells, we first downregulated Alr in mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) using pooled siRNA and demonstrated a significant reduction of Alr at the mRNA level (Figure 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Three out of four siRNAs in the pooled siRNA target regions shared by the full-length and short isoform of ALR.
source: Of note, three out of the four siRNAs in the pooled siRNA target regions shared by the full-length and the short isoform of ALR, and we observed reduction of protein levels of both isoforms (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Stated in text and confirmed by western blot data in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Downregulation of Alr reduces protein levels of both ALR isoforms.
source: Of note, three out of the four siRNAs in the pooled siRNA target regions shared by the full-length and the short isoform of ALR, and we observed reduction of protein levels of both isoforms (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot data in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Downregulation of Alr in MEFs does not result in significant cell death at 72 hr.
source: While previous literature in moue embryonic stem cell described significant cell death after Alr downregulation (Todd et al., 2010), we did not observe significant cell death at 72 hr after downregulation of Alr (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Demonstrated by cell death assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Downregulation of Alr decreased GPAT protein levels.
source: Downregulation of Alr decreased GPAT protein levels (Figure 1C), and reduced XO (Figure 1D) and cytosolic aconitase activity (Figure 1E).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Downregulation of Alr reduced XO activity.
source: Downregulation of Alr decreased GPAT protein levels (Figure 1C), and reduced XO (Figure 1D) and cytosolic aconitase activity (Figure 1E).
evidence: Demonstrated by enzyme activity assay data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Downregulation of Alr reduced cytosolic aconitase activity.
source: Downregulation of Alr decreased GPAT protein levels (Figure 1C), and reduced XO (Figure 1D) and cytosolic aconitase activity (Figure 1E).
evidence: Demonstrated by enzyme activity assay data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Downregulation of Alr does not change complex I activity.
source: We also measured the activity of the Fe/S cluster-containing mitochondrial complexes I and II, and found no change in complex I and II activity with Alr downregulation (Figure 1F and G).
evidence: Demonstrated by enzyme activity assay data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Downregulation of Alr does not change complex II activity.
source: We also measured the activity of the Fe/S cluster-containing mitochondrial complexes I and II, and found no change in complex I and II activity with Alr downregulation (Figure 1F and G).
evidence: Demonstrated by enzyme activity assay data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Downregulation of Alr does not affect mitochondrial oxygen consumption.
source: To further assess mitochondrial function, we measured oxygen consumption in intact cells fueled with glucose and L-glutamine using Seahorse Extracellular Flux Assay, and did not observe significant difference in mitochondrial oxygen consumption (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Demonstrated by Seahorse assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Acute reduction in ALR impairs specifically cytosolic Fe/S cluster maturation in mammalian cells.
source: Our results therefore demonstrated that acute reduction in ALR impairs specifically cytosolic Fe/S cluster maturation in mammalian cells similar to the previously published yeast studies.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of reduced cytosolic Fe/S markers and unchanged mitochondrial complex activities.

claim: Downregulation of Alr increases Tfrc mRNA levels in wild type MEFs.
source: Transferrin receptor-1 (Tfrc) mRNA levels were increased in wild type MEFs with Alr downregulation (Figure 2A).
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Downregulation of Alr increases transferrin-mediated iron uptake.
source: Consistent with changes in Tfrc expression, we also observed an increase in transferrin-mediated iron uptake in cells treated with Alr siRNA (Figure 2B).
evidence: Demonstrated by 55Fe-transferrin uptake assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Downregulation of Alr results in higher steady state levels of iron in both the cytoplasm and mitochondria.
source: The increased iron uptake resulted in higher steady state levels of iron in both the cytoplasm and mitochondria (Figure 2C), similar to other genetic models with cytosolic Fe/S cluster maturation defects (Sato et al., 2011; Ichikawa et al., 2012).
evidence: Demonstrated by steady-state 55Fe measurement data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Downregulation of Alr does not change Tfrc promoter activity.
source: We first generated a luciferase reporter construct harboring 700 base pairs of the Tfrc promoter upstream of the Tfrc transcription start site (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A). Downregulation of Alr did not change luciferase activity of this construct (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that ALR does not regulate Tfrc expression at the transcriptional level.
evidence: Demonstrated by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: ALR does not regulate Tfrc expression at the transcriptional level.
source: Downregulation of Alr did not change luciferase activity of this construct (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that ALR does not regulate Tfrc expression at the transcriptional level.
evidence: Inferred from lack of change in Tfrc promoter reporter activity with ALR downregulation.

claim: Downregulation of Alr increases luciferase activity of full-length Tfrc 3'-UTR reporter.
source: We next made a construct containing the full-length Tfrc 3'-UTR downstream of luciferase cDNA (Figure 2D). Luciferase activity of this reporter increased with iron chelation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), and with Alr downregulation (Figure 2E), suggesting that ALR posttranscriptionally regulates Tfrc through stabilization of Tfrc mRNA.
evidence: Demonstrated by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: ALR posttranscriptionally regulates Tfrc through stabilization of Tfrc mRNA.
source: Luciferase activity of this reporter increased with iron chelation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), and with Alr downregulation (Figure 2E), suggesting that ALR posttranscriptionally regulates Tfrc through stabilization of Tfrc mRNA.
evidence: Inferred from increased activity of Tfrc 3'-UTR reporter with ALR downregulation.

claim: Downregulation of Alr has no effect on the luciferase activity of the IRE-deleted Tfrc 3'-UTR reporter construct.
source: Furthermore, downregulation of Alr had no effect on the luciferase activity of the IRE-deleted reporter construct (Figure 2F), suggesting that activation of the IRP/IRE system is required for the effects of ALR on cellular iron homeostasis.
evidence: Demonstrated by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Activation of the IRP/IRE system is required for the effects of ALR on cellular iron homeostasis.
source: Furthermore, downregulation of Alr had no effect on the luciferase activity of the IRE-deleted reporter construct (Figure 2F), suggesting that activation of the IRP/IRE system is required for the effects of ALR on cellular iron homeostasis.
evidence: Inferred from lack of effect of ALR downregulation on IRE-deleted reporter.

claim: Alr knockdown in Ireb2 KO MEFs results in a significant increase in Tfrc mRNA levels.
source: Alr knockdown in these cells resulted in a significant reduction in ALR protein levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), and a significant increase in Tfrc mRNA levels and transferrin-mediated iron uptake (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F and G), suggesting that the regulation of Tfrc by ALR is independent of IRP2.
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Alr knockdown in Ireb2 KO MEFs results in a significant increase in transferrin-mediated iron uptake.
source: Alr knockdown in these cells resulted in a significant reduction in ALR protein levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), and a significant increase in Tfrc mRNA levels and transferrin-mediated iron uptake (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F and G), suggesting that the regulation of Tfrc by ALR is independent of IRP2.
evidence: Demonstrated by iron uptake assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The regulation of Tfrc by ALR is independent of IRP2.
source: Alr knockdown in these cells resulted in a significant reduction in ALR protein levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), and a significant increase in Tfrc mRNA levels and transferrin-mediated iron uptake (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F and G), suggesting that the regulation of Tfrc by ALR is independent of IRP2.
evidence: Inferred from persistent Tfrc upregulation in Ireb2 KO cells with ALR downregulation.

claim: Treatment of Aco1 KD MEFs with Alr siRNA does not increase Tfrc mRNA levels.
source: Although treatment of Aco1 KD MEFs with Alr siRNA significantly reduced Alr mRNA levels (Figure 2G), Tfrc mRNA levels and TFRC-mediated iron uptake were not increased (Figure 2G and H).
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Treatment of Aco1 KD MEFs with Alr siRNA does not increase TFRC-mediated iron uptake.
source: Although treatment of Aco1 KD MEFs with Alr siRNA significantly reduced Alr mRNA levels (Figure 2G), Tfrc mRNA levels and TFRC-mediated iron uptake were not increased (Figure 2G and H).
evidence: Demonstrated by iron uptake assay data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Alr downregulation impairs Fe/S cluster maturation and subsequently promotes increases in Tfrc mRNA and cellular iron levels in an IRP1-dependent manner.
source: Since IRP1 is activated upon losing its mature Fe/S cluster, our results indicate that Alr downregulation impairs Fe/S cluster maturation and subsequently promotes increases in Tfrc mRNA and cellular iron levels in an IRP1-dependent manner.
evidence: Inferred from the requirement of IRP1 but not IRP2 for ALR-mediated regulation of Tfrc.

claim: Overexpression of the full-length but not the short isoform of ALR rescues the increase in Tfrc mRNA levels caused by Alr downregulation.
source: Overexpression of the full-length (predominantly mitochondrial) but not the short (cytosolic) isoform of ALR rescued the increase in Tfrc mRNA levels and transferrin-dependent iron uptake (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Overexpression of the full-length but not the short isoform of ALR rescues the increase in transferrin-dependent iron uptake caused by Alr downregulation.
source: Overexpression of the full-length (predominantly mitochondrial) but not the short (cytosolic) isoform of ALR rescued the increase in Tfrc mRNA levels and transferrin-dependent iron uptake (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Demonstrated by iron uptake assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Re-expression of the full-length but not the cytosolic isoform of ALR reverses reduced cytosolic aconitase activity caused by Alr downregulation.
source: In addition, the cytosolic Fe/S cluster maturation defects, including reduced cytosolic aconitase and XO activity, and decreased GPAT protein levels, were all reversed by the re-expression of the full-length but not the cytosolic isoform of ALR (Figure 3C–F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Demonstrated by enzyme activity assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Re-expression of the full-length but not the cytosolic isoform of ALR reverses reduced XO activity caused by Alr downregulation.
source: In addition, the cytosolic Fe/S cluster maturation defects, including reduced cytosolic aconitase and XO activity, and decreased GPAT protein levels, were all reversed by the re-expression of the full-length but not the cytosolic isoform of ALR (Figure 3C–F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Demonstrated by enzyme activity assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Re-expression of the full-length but not the cytosolic isoform of ALR reverses decreased GPAT protein levels caused by Alr downregulation.
source: In addition, the cytosolic Fe/S cluster maturation defects, including reduced cytosolic aconitase and XO activity, and decreased GPAT protein levels, were all reversed by the re-expression of the full-length but not the cytosolic isoform of ALR (Figure 3C–F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot data shown in Figure 3E and 3F.

claim: The full-length ALR isoform regulates cytosolic Fe/S cluster maturation, which in turn affects IRP1 activity and cellular iron levels.
source: These observations indicate that the full-length ALR isoform regulates cytosolic Fe/S cluster maturation, which in turn affects IRP1 activity and cellular iron levels.
evidence: Inferred from isoform-specific rescue experiments showing only full-length ALR rescues Fe/S and iron phenotypes.

claim: ALR downregulation does not change the mRNA levels of ABCB7 and ABCB8 in HEK293 cells.
source: However, the mRNA levels of ABCB7 and ABCB8 (Figure 4A) and total cellular ABCB7 and ABCB8 protein levels (Figure 4B and C) did not change with ALR downregulation.
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: ALR downregulation does not change total cellular ABCB7 protein levels.
source: However, the mRNA levels of ABCB7 and ABCB8 (Figure 4A) and total cellular ABCB7 and ABCB8 protein levels (Figure 4B and C) did not change with ALR downregulation.
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: ALR downregulation does not change total cellular ABCB8 protein levels.
source: However, the mRNA levels of ABCB7 and ABCB8 (Figure 4A) and total cellular ABCB7 and ABCB8 protein levels (Figure 4B and C) did not change with ALR downregulation.
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: ALR downregulation does not change the mitochondrial level of ABCB7.
source: ALR downregulation did not change the mitochondrial level of ABCB7 (Figure 4D), but caused a significant reduction in mitochondrial ABCB8 (Figure 4E).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot of mitochondrial fraction shown in Figure 4D.

claim: ALR downregulation causes a significant reduction in mitochondrial ABCB8.
source: ALR downregulation did not change the mitochondrial level of ABCB7 (Figure 4D), but caused a significant reduction in mitochondrial ABCB8 (Figure 4E).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot of mitochondrial fraction shown in Figure 4E.

claim: ABCB7 overexpression does not rescue the increase in Tfrc expression in ALR-downregulated MEFs.
source: Additionally, ABCB7 overexpression did not rescue the increase in Tfrc expression in ALR-downregulated MEFs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E), demonstrating lack of functional overlap between ABCB7 and ABCB8.
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: There is a lack of functional overlap between ABCB7 and ABCB8.
source: Additionally, ABCB7 overexpression did not rescue the increase in Tfrc expression in ALR-downregulated MEFs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E), demonstrating lack of functional overlap between ABCB7 and ABCB8.
evidence: Inferred from inability of ABCB7 overexpression to rescue ALR downregulation phenotype.

claim: ALR may be required for the mitochondrial import of ABCB8 but not ABCB7.
source: These results suggest that ALR may be required for the mitochondrial import of ABCB8 but not ABCB7.
evidence: Inferred from selective reduction of mitochondrial ABCB8 but not ABCB7 with ALR downregulation.

claim: ALR downregulation decreases the mitochondrial import of newly synthesized MIA40.
source: We first validated our assay system by showing that the mitochondrial import of newly synthesized MIA40 was decreased with ALR downregulation (Figure 5A).
evidence: Demonstrated by doxycycline-inducible import assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Mitochondrial import of SU9-eGFP does not change with ALR downregulation.
source: As expected, mitochondrial import of the His-tagged SU9-eGFP did not change with ALR downregulation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Demonstrated by doxycycline-inducible import assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: ALR downregulation results in reduced mitochondrial import of ABCB8.
source: We then studied the effects of ALR downregulation on the mitochondrial import of ABCB7 and ABCB8. ALR downregulation resulted in reduced mitochondrial import of ABCB8 (Figure 5B), but not ABCB7 (Figure 5C).
evidence: Demonstrated by doxycycline-inducible import assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: ALR downregulation does not affect mitochondrial import of ABCB7.
source: We then studied the effects of ALR downregulation on the mitochondrial import of ABCB7 and ABCB8. ALR downregulation resulted in reduced mitochondrial import of ABCB8 (Figure 5B), but not ABCB7 (Figure 5C).
evidence: Demonstrated by doxycycline-inducible import assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: ALR downregulation impairs the mitochondrial import of ABCB8, which in turn affects cytosolic Fe/S cluster maturation.
source: These findings suggest that ALR downregulation impairs the mitochondrial import of ABCB8, which in turn affects cytosolic Fe/S cluster maturation.
evidence: Inferred from combination of reduced ABCB8 import and cytosolic Fe/S defects with ALR downregulation.

claim: MIA40 downregulation results in increased TFRC expression in HEK293 cells.
source: We first confirmed that MIA40 downregulation in HEK293 cells resulted in increased TFRC expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D and E), similar to what we observed with ALR downregulation (Figure 2A).
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: MIA40 downregulation decreases mitochondrial import of ALR.
source: In cells with MIA40 downregulation, we observed a decrease in mitochondrial import of ALR, a known substrate of MIA40 (Kallergi et al., 2012), but not SU9-eGFP (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Demonstrated by doxycycline-inducible import assay data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: MIA40 downregulation does not affect mitochondrial import of SU9-eGFP.
source: In cells with MIA40 downregulation, we observed a decrease in mitochondrial import of ALR, a known substrate of MIA40 (Kallergi et al., 2012), but not SU9-eGFP (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Demonstrated by doxycycline-inducible import assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F.

claim: MIA40 downregulation impairs mitochondrial import of ABCB8.
source: Similar to our finding with ALR downregulation, MIA40 downregulation impaired mitochondrial import of ABCB8 but not ABCB7 (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: Demonstrated by doxycycline-inducible import assay data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: MIA40 downregulation does not impair mitochondrial import of ABCB7.
source: Similar to our finding with ALR downregulation, MIA40 downregulation impaired mitochondrial import of ABCB8 but not ABCB7 (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: Demonstrated by doxycycline-inducible import assay data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Mitochondrial import of ABCB8 requires both MIA40 and ALR.
source: These observations collectively indicate that mitochondrial import of ABCB8 requires both MIA40 and ALR.
evidence: Inferred from impaired ABCB8 import with either ALR or MIA40 downregulation.

claim: Downregulation of TIM23 results in decreased mitochondrial import of ABCB8.
source: Downregulation of TIM23 (an integral protein of the TIM23 complex) resulted in decreased mitochondrial import of both SU9-eGFP (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G, positive control) and ABCB8 (Figure 5G), while the mitochondrial import of MIA40 (the negative control) was not affected (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Demonstrated by doxycycline-inducible import assay data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Dissipation of mitochondrial membrane potential decreases mitochondrial transport of ABCB8.
source: Additionally, dissipation of mitochondrial membrane potential, a required factor for TIM23-mediated protein transport (Jensen and Dunn, 2002), decreased mitochondrial transport of SU9eGFP and ABCB8 (Figure 5H and Figure 5—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: Demonstrated by CCCP treatment experiment shown in Figure 5H.

claim: After passing through the outer mitochondrial membrane, ABCB8 peptide interacts with the MIA40 protein import complex prior to being transported to the inner mitochondrial membrane by the TIM23 complex.
source: These results collectively support a model in which, after passing through the outer mitochondrial membrane, ABCB8 peptide interacts with the MIA40 protein import complex prior to being transported to the inner mitochondrial membrane by the TIM23 complex.
evidence: Inferred from the dual dependence of ABCB8 import on both MIA40/ALR and TIM23 systems.

claim: Endogenous ABCB8 copurifies with MIA40.
source: To test whether ABCB8 directly interacts with MIA40, we overexpressed C-terminal His-tagged MIA40 in HEK293 cells and loaded the isolated mitochondrial lysate onto a Ni-NTA column to pull down MIA40 and its interacting proteins. Endogenous ABCB8 copurified with MIA40 (Figure 6A), suggesting that ABCB8 interacts with MIA40 during its translocation into the mitochondria.
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: ABCB8 interacts with MIA40 during its translocation into the mitochondria.
source: Endogenous ABCB8 copurified with MIA40 (Figure 6A), suggesting that ABCB8 interacts with MIA40 during its translocation into the mitochondria.
evidence: Inferred from co-immunoprecipitation results showing physical interaction.

claim: Mutation of either or both of the two cysteine residues in MIA40 abolishes the interaction between MIA40 and ABCB8.
source: Mutation of either or both of the two cysteine residues in MIA40, which have been shown to be required for substrate interaction (Peleh et al., 2016), abolished the interaction between MIA40 and ABCB8 (Figure 6B).
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation data with MIA40 cysteine mutants shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Five cysteine residues in ABCB8 are highly conserved in vertebrates.
source: We first performed alignment of ABCB8 protein sequences in vertebrates, and identified five highly conserved cysteine residues (Figure 6C).
evidence: Demonstrated by sequence alignment shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Mutation of all five conserved cysteines to serines greatly diminishes the interaction of ABCB8 to MIA40.
source: While mutating each of these residues had minimal effect on the interaction between ABCB8 and MIA40 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), mutation of all five cysteines to serines (5CS-ABCB8) greatly diminished the interaction of ABCB8 to MIA40 (Figure 6D).
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation data with ABCB8 5CS mutant shown in Figure 6D.

claim: DTT greatly diminishes the interaction between MIA40 and ABCB8.
source: To further support this model, we perform pulldown experiment of wild type MIA40 and ABCB8 in the presence of 100 mM dithiothreitol (DTT). DTT greatly diminished the interaction between MIA40 and ABCB8 (Figure 6E), similar to the 5CS mutant.
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation data with DTT treatment shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The five conserved cysteine residues are not conserved between ABCB7 and ABCB8.
source: The five conserved cysteine residues are not conserved between ABCB7 and ABCB8 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), thereby explaining the differential dependency of MIA40/ALR protein import system on mitochondrial import of these two proteins.
evidence: Demonstrated by sequence alignment shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The five conserved cysteine residues are collectively needed for recognition by MIA40.
source: Thus, these five cysteine residues are collectively needed for recognition by MIA40, and the absence of one is not sufficient to disrupt the interaction between ABCB8 and MIA40.
evidence: Inferred from the requirement of mutating all five cysteines to abolish MIA40 interaction.

claim: MIA40 and ABCB8 interact through disulfide bond formation.
source: Taken together, these observations suggest that MIA40 and ABCB8 interact through disulfide bond formation.
evidence: Inferred from cysteine mutation and DTT treatment experiments disrupting the interaction.

claim: Through its role in mitochondrial intermembrane space, ALR is critical for cytosolic Fe/S cluster biogenesis.
source: We hereby demonstrated that through its role in mitochondrial intermembrane space, ALR is critical for cytosolic Fe/S cluster biogenesis.
evidence: Demonstrated through multiple experiments showing ALR's role in ABCB8 import and cytosolic Fe/S maturation.

claim: Downregulation of ALR prevents mitochondrial import of ABCB8, which can result in cytosolic Fe/S cluster maturation defects.
source: Importantly, we discovered that downregulation of ALR prevents mitochondrial import of ABCB8, which in turn can result in cytosolic Fe/S cluster maturation defects.
evidence: Demonstrated through import assays and Fe/S cluster measurements.

claim: The role of ALR in the maturation of cytosolic Fe/S cluster proteins in mammalian systems depends on its localization to the mitochondria.
source: Although ALR localizes to various compartments of the cells, our data strongly indicate that the role of ALR in the maturation of cytosolic Fe/S cluster proteins in mammalian systems depends on its localization to the mitochondria and its function in the MIA40/ALR protein import pathway.
evidence: Demonstrated through isoform-specific rescue experiments showing only mitochondrial ALR rescues the phenotype.

claim: The role of ALR in the maturation of cytosolic Fe/S cluster proteins in mammalian systems depends on its function in the MIA40/ALR protein import pathway.
source: Although ALR localizes to various compartments of the cells, our data strongly indicate that the role of ALR in the maturation of cytosolic Fe/S cluster proteins in mammalian systems depends on its localization to the mitochondria and its function in the MIA40/ALR protein import pathway.
evidence: Demonstrated through experiments showing MIA40 downregulation phenocopies ALR downregulation.

claim: ALR downregulation impairs mitochondrial import of ABCB8 protein.
source: Our mechanistic studies demonstrated that ALR downregulation impairs mitochondrial import of ABCB8 protein, and decreased ABCB8 levels have been shown to cause defective cytosolic Fe/S cluster maturation (Ichikawa et al., 2012).
evidence: Demonstrated through import assays and mitochondrial fractionation experiments.

claim: Decreased mitochondrial ABCB8 level and ensued cytosolic Fe/S cluster maturation defect activate IRP1 and increase cellular iron uptake.
source: This decreased mitochondrial ABCB8 level and ensued cytosolic Fe/S cluster maturation defect activate IRP1 and increase cellular iron uptake.
evidence: Demonstrated through measurements of Tfrc expression, iron uptake, and IRP1-dependence experiments.

claim: Reduction in mitochondrial ABCB8 levels is associated with increased sensitivity of cells to oxidative stress.
source: Additionally, reduction in mitochondrial ABCB8 levels is also associated with increased sensitivity of cells to oxidative stress (Ichikawa et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Elevated iron level has been causally linked to the cardiomyopathy phenotype in mice with cardiac-specific ABCB8 deletion.
source: It is also worth pointing out that elevated iron level has been causally linked to the cardiomyopathy phenotype in mice with cardiac-specific ABCB8 deletion (Chang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to published mouse study.

claim: Not all reported patients with ALR mutations have complex IV deficiency.
source: First of all, not all reported patients with ALR mutations have complex IV deficiency.
evidence: Based on review of published patient reports.

claim: Chronic mitochondrial iron overload has been linked to mitochondrial damage.
source: Chronic mitochondrial iron overload, a cellular response seen in many models of cytoplasmic Fe/S cluster maturation defects (Lange et al., 2001; Pondarré et al., 2006; Ichikawa et al., 2012), has been linked to mitochondrial damage.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Extensive mitochondrial damage has been demonstrated in tissue samples from patients with ALR mutations.
source: Extensive mitochondrial damage has also been demonstrated in tissue samples from patients with ALR mutations (Nambot et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to published patient study.

claim: Respiratory chain deficiency in patients with ALR mutations is likely to be a secondary effect of chronic cytoplasmic Fe/S cluster deficiency.
source: Taken together, respiratory chain deficiency in those patients is likely to be a secondary effect of chronic cytoplasmic Fe/S cluster deficiency.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of acute vs. chronic effects and known consequences of Fe/S deficiency.

claim: Downregulation of MIA40 or ALR does not affect mitochondrial import of the canonical TIM23 complex substrate SU9-eGFP.
source: However, downregulation of MIA40 or ALR does not affect mitochondrial import of the canonical TIM23 complex substrate SU9-eGFP (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D), and the function of the Tim23 complex was not altered in yeast lacking Mia40 (Wrobel et al., 2013).
evidence: Demonstrated by import assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D, and supported by citation.

claim: The function of the Tim23 complex was not altered in yeast lacking Mia40.
source: However, downregulation of MIA40 or ALR does not affect mitochondrial import of the canonical TIM23 complex substrate SU9-eGFP (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D), and the function of the Tim23 complex was not altered in yeast lacking Mia40 (Wrobel et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to published yeast study.

claim: Modulation of MIA40/ALR complex likely affects the mitochondrial import of ABCB8 upstream of TIM23 and import into the inner mitochondrial membrane.
source: Therefore, modulation of MIA40/ALR complex likely affects the mitochondrial of ABCB8 import upstream of TIM23 and import into the inner mitochondrial membrane.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of effect on TIM23 function but requirement for ABCB8 import.

claim: A nascent ABCB8 peptide interacts with the MIA40/ALR import system and TIM23 complex sequentially during mitochondrial import.
source: We thus propose a model where a nascent ABCB8 peptide interacts with the MIA40/ALR import system and TIM23 complex sequentially during mitochondrial import, similar to the mechanism that is reported for p53 and Mrp10 for mitochondrial import (Zhuang et al., 2013; Longen et al., 2014).
evidence: Proposed model based on experimental data and analogy to published mechanisms for other proteins.

claim: ABCB8 is a novel substrate for the MIA40/ALR protein import system.
source: Our results demonstrate physical interaction between MIA40 and ABCB8 and suggest that ABCB8 is a novel substrate for the MIA40/ALR protein import system.
evidence: Demonstrated through co-immunoprecipitation and import assays.

claim: The five conserved cysteines in ABCB8 likely play a redundant function in the interaction between MIA40 and ABCB8.
source: These cysteines likely play a redundant function in the interaction between MIA40 and ABCB8, as the physical interaction between these ABCB8 and MIA40 did not diminish until all five cysteines were mutated.
evidence: Inferred from mutagenesis experiments showing individual mutations have minimal effect.

claim: The five conserved cysteines in ABCB8 do not form a CX2C or a CX9C consensus motif characteristic of most MIA40 substrates.
source: It is worth noting that the five conserved cysteines, or any other cysteine residues in ABCB8, do not form a CX2C or a CX9C consensus motif that is characteristic of most MIA40 substrates (Sideris et al., 2009).
evidence: Based on sequence analysis and comparison to known MIA40 substrate motifs.

claim: Not all five conserved cysteines in ABCB8 are conserved in lower vertebrates such as zebrafish and Xenopus.
source: However, not all five cysteines are conserved in lower vertebrates such as zebrafish and Xenopus.
evidence: Based on sequence alignment analysis across species.

claim: The proposed mechanism linking ALR to ABCB8 import is likely a late product of evolution.
source: Therefore, our proposed mechanism is likely a late product of evolution and a similar mechanism may not exist in yeast.
evidence: Inferred from lack of conservation of all five cysteines in lower vertebrates and lack of clear ABCB8 homolog in yeast.

claim: Cytosolic Fe/S cluster maturation in mammalian cells depends on the mitochondrial isoform of ALR.
source: In summary, we demonstrated that cytosolic Fe/S cluster maturation in mammalian cells depends on the mitochondrial isoform of ALR, which mediates the transport of ABCB8 into mitochondria.
evidence: Demonstrated through isoform-specific rescue experiments and import assays.

claim: ALR plays a role in cellular iron regulation through indirectly regulating IRP1 activity.
source: ALR thus plays a role in cellular iron regulation through indirectly regulating IRP1 activity.
evidence: Demonstrated through experiments showing IRP1-dependent regulation of Tfrc by ALR.

claim: Sequence variation in conserved cysteine residues in ABCB7 and ABCB8 may explain why the mitochondrial import of only ABCB8 but not ABCB7 depends on the MIA40/ALR pathway.
source: Sequence variation in conserved cysteine residues in ABCB7 and ABCB8 may explain why the mitochondrial import of only ABCB8 but not ABCB7 depends on the MIA40/ALR pathway.
evidence: Inferred from sequence alignment showing lack of conservation of the five cysteines between ABCB7 and ABCB8.
